source: Oudeyer & Kaplan (2007) What is intrinsic motivation? A typology of computational approaches
finding: Splits intrinsic motivation into knowledge-based, competence-based and morphological families. Knowledge-based models reward the gap between experience and the agent's expectations. Two branches: information-theoretic (distributions) and predictive (error of a predictor).
numbers: Typology lists UM, IGM, ILNM, LPM, SM, FM, IM, CPM, CM and others. Authors rate LPM, IGM and CPM as the most promising (both high exploration and high organization potential).
quote: Intrinsic motivation is defined as the doing of an activity for its inherent satisfaction rather than for some separable consequence.
limits: Typology is conceptual, no new experiments; a 2009 chapter version exists.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean vocabulary for any curiosity operator: novelty, surprise, familiarity and progress are different rewards on the same error signal.

source: Oudeyer & Kaplan (2007) typology: predictive novelty and its fixes
finding: Predictive novelty reward is r = C * prediction error (Eq 9). Problem: pure noise gives endless error. Fix 1: reward intermediate error with a Gaussian bump around a threshold (Eq 10). Fix 2: reward the ratio of actual to expected error (surprise, Eq 15).
numbers: Eq 9 r=C*Er; Eq 10 r=C1*exp(-C2*(Er-Er*)^2); Eq 15 r=C*Er/Meta-predicted Er; familiarity Eq 16 r=C/Er.
limits: Authors say the single threshold in Eq 10 is tuned by the engineer by intuition and is a drawback.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent, raw most-surprising is a trap; reward must discount error that cannot be reduced.

source: Oudeyer & Kaplan (2007) typology: learning progress motivation (LPM) formula
finding: Learning progress is the decrease of prediction error over time inside a region: r = mean error over the older window minus mean error over the recent window (Eq 11). Regions group similar situations so comparison is meaningful. Schmidhuber 1991 version: error before vs just after one update on the same input.
numbers: Eq 11: r(SM(t)) = Er_Rn(t - tau) - Er_Rn(t), averaged over the last theta predictions in region Rn.
limits: Naive global comparison would reward moving from a leaf in the wind to a white wall. Needs a region-splitting mechanism and a low learning rate.
agent_relevance: Progress must be computed per task-type or topic, not over the whole stream. A scaffold can track error by problem class.

source: Oudeyer & Kaplan (2007) typology: summary table of models
finding: Figure 7 rates each model by exploration potential, organization potential, compute cost and number of existing implementations (stars, 1 to 3).
numbers: ILNM: exploration 2 stars, organization 2. LPM: 3 stars exploration, 3 stars organization. FM: 1 star exploration, 3 stars organization. IM and CPM: 3 stars exploration. The ratings are rough author estimates.
limits: Subjective ratings, no measurement.
agent_relevance: Supports choosing progress-style rewards over plain novelty for open-ended exploration.

source: Oudeyer, Kaplan & Hafner (2007) Intrinsic motivation systems for autonomous mental development
finding: Introduces Intelligent Adaptive Curiosity (IAC). The robot splits its sensorimotor space into regions with an expert predictor each, tracks the error list per region, and gets reward equal to the drop in smoothed error (learning progress). It avoids both too predictable and too unpredictable regions as a side effect.
numbers: Regions split recursively when exemplar count passes a threshold, choosing the cut that minimises summed variance. Prediction with 3,000,000 exemplars takes about 17 scalar comparisons per query.
quote: keeps, as a side effect, the robot away both from situations which are too predictable and from situations which are too unpredictable
limits: One-step lookahead only, no delayed intrinsic reward. Needs a low learning rate for the before/after error comparison to work (as Schmidhuber 2010 points out).
agent_relevance: Region + expert + progress is a template for a per-topic competence tracker that ignores noise topics.

source: Oudeyer, Kaplan & Hafner (2007) simulated robot with three zones (Webots)
finding: A simulated robot chooses sound frequencies. One zone is pure noise, one is easy to learn, one is harder to learn. IAC ends up avoiding noise, doing the easy zone first, then moving to the harder one.
numbers: Run of 5000 time steps. Stage 1 uniform actions. Stage 2 after the first 250 steps focuses on the easy-to-learn zone. Stage 3 shifts to the more complex zone. Noise zone avoided throughout.
quote: the robot consistently avoids the situations in which nothing can be learned, begins by easy situations, and then shifts autonomously to a more complex situation
limits: Toy setup, one run described in this section, no statistics over many seeds.
agent_relevance: Shows a self-made curriculum from error trends alone, with no hand-set difficulty.

source: Oudeyer, Kaplan & Hafner (2007) Playground Experiment (Sony AIBO)
finding: A real AIBO on a baby play mat with a bitable and a bashable object. With IAC alone it passes through ordered phases: random actions, just looking, biting without affordance, bashing without affordance, looking at an object, biting with affordance, bashing with affordance.
numbers: Peaks A to G in action-frequency windows of 100 steps and gaze windows of 200 steps. Order of focus matches rising dimensionality: look (pan, tilt), bite (adds crouch depth), bash (adds angle and strength). Non-affordant use came before affordant use in the runs described.
limits: Regularities are statistical. Fig 9 shows atypical runs, e.g. bashing focus before biting, or affordant bashing very early. No success rates over many runs in the text read.
agent_relevance: Stage-like order of exploration emerges from progress rewards; a model for ordering sub-skills in an agent.

source: Schmidhuber (2010) Formal theory of creativity, fun, and intrinsic motivation (1990-2010)
finding: Curiosity reward should be the first derivative of the model's quality (compression progress), not the prediction error. Error-based reward fails because random noise never becomes predictable. Reviews implementations from 1991, 1995 and 1997-2002.
numbers: 1991: reward = predictor improvement, with a confidence-network version. 1995: reward = KL divergence between predictor posterior and prior (information gain). 1997-2002: zero-sum intrinsic reward games between two modules that bet on experiment outcomes.
limits: Theory is general but mostly unmeasured; few new numbers in this review. Universal version is not computable in practice.
agent_relevance: Direct origin of the learning-progress idea this subfield rests on.

source: Schmidhuber (2010) critique of Oudeyer's IAC and of free-energy agents
finding: Claims IAC is a special case of the 1991 Adaptive Curiosity system, restricted to one-step lookahead with no delayed intrinsic reward. Says the 1991 system already handles stochastic input because the predictor shows no net change there. Argues free-energy-minimising agents prefer predictable states and would sit in a dark room, while progress-driven agents leave it.
numbers: Quotes Oudeyer et al: before/after error comparison only works for a low learning rate and can be sensitive to stochastic fluctuations.
limits: Priority dispute told from one side (Schmidhuber's own review). Oudeyer's regional evaluation is not the same mechanism as the 1991 one.
agent_relevance: Test for our agent: does it keep exploring a fully solved topic? A progress reward says no.

source: Kaplan & Oudeyer (2004) Maximizing learning progress: an internal reward system for development
finding: Early proposal of a learning-progress reward for a developing robot, cited in the 2007 papers as the first Kaplan and Oudeyer implementation. Not opened this session.
limits: Not read; known only through citations in opened papers.
agent_relevance: Foundational citation only.

source: Schmidhuber (1991) A possibility for implementing curiosity and boredom in model-building neural controllers
finding: Original adaptive curiosity: reward the controller for improvements of the world model, not for its errors. Known here only through Schmidhuber 2010.
limits: Not opened; second hand via the 2010 review.
agent_relevance: Original source of progress-based curiosity.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: A pseudo-count from a density model gives a generalised visit count. Pseudo-counts connect count bonuses to information gain via prediction gain, a variant of Schmidhuber's compression progress. The bonus improves exploration on hard Atari games.
numbers: On Montezuma's Revenge the agent averages a score of 2461 at one point and 3439 by 100 million frames (higher than prior published results per the paper). Freeway test: pseudo-count near zero on the first salient event.
limits: Bonus helps hard-exploration games; life-loss signal was detrimental in Montezuma. Numbers read from the text and appendix, not all games.
agent_relevance: Counts and progress are two views of one quantity; a count of how often a reasoning pattern was tried is a cheap stand-in.

source: Achiam & Sastry (2017) Surprise-based intrinsic motivation for deep RL
finding: Defines surprise as KL divergence of the true transition from the learned model. Two cheap approximations: surprisal (negative log prob of next state) and k-step learning progress. Matches VIME at far lower compute.
numbers: Tested on 5 continuous-control tasks plus 4 Atari RAM games, 10 runs with fixed seeds. Surprisal gave good results in all domains. Learning progress k=1 worked on CartpoleSwingup and HalfCheetah but faltered in the others. Both beat reported VIME on HalfCheetah; both scored below VIME on CartpoleSwingup; surprisal about equal to VIME on SwimmerGather after 1000 iterations.
limits: Learning progress failed on MountainCar because the dynamics model converged and rewards became identically zero. Median over 10 runs only.
agent_relevance: Head-to-head: raw surprisal was more robust than progress in these tasks. Progress is not a free win.

source: Pathak et al. (2017) Curiosity-driven exploration by self-supervised prediction (ICM)
finding: Intrinsic reward is the forward-model error in a feature space learned by an inverse model, so the agent ignores things it cannot affect. Works in VizDoom and Super Mario Bros with no extrinsic reward.
numbers: VizDoom sparse setting: ICM+A3C 100% (100%), VIME+TRPO 46.1% (27.1%), TRPO 26.0% (0.0%), A3C 0.0%. Very sparse: ICM reached a perfect score in 66% of random runs; A3C and pixel-based ICM never did. With 40% of the image replaced by white noise, ICM still succeeded; pixel ICM suffered. No-reward Mario: crossed over 30% of Level-1.
limits: Noise test uses a fixed noise region that does not depend on the agent, not an action-controlled noise source. Policy trained on Level-1 'as is' did not do well on Level-2.
agent_relevance: Predict only what the agent can influence. For an LLM, ignore error from parts of text the agent cannot change.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-scale study of curiosity-driven learning
finding: Pure curiosity, no extrinsic reward and no end-of-episode signal, across 54 environments (48 Atari games, Mario, Roboschool, Pong, Unity mazes). Random features work surprisingly well.
numbers: Pixel-based dynamics curiosity worked poorly everywhere. Inverse-dynamics features beat random features in 55% of Atari games. Curious agent beat a random agent in about 75% of Atari games; random-feature version in 70%.
limits: Agents chase game score only when score correlates with novelty. Random features generalise worse to new Mario levels than learned ones.
agent_relevance: Large-scale evidence that prediction-error curiosity alone gives non-trivial behaviour, but depends on feature choice.

source: Burda et al. (2018) noisy-TV experiment
finding: A TV that changes channel on action was added to a Unity maze. It drastically slowed learning of both IDF and RF curiosity agents.
numbers: Authors note that with a long enough run the agents sometimes converge to getting the extrinsic reward consistently.
limits: Single maze, qualitative curves.
agent_relevance: Empirical proof that the noisy-TV thought experiment is a real failure mode for error-based curiosity.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by random network distillation (RND)
finding: Bonus is the error of a network predicting a fixed random network's output. The target is deterministic and inside the learner's function class, so stochastic noise and model limits do not inflate the bonus. Non-episodic intrinsic return improves exploration.
numbers: Pure-intrinsic agent finds more than half the rooms in Montezuma's Revenge. Best agent often finds 22 of 24 rooms on level one and occasionally passes it. A table row shows RND at 8,152 on Montezuma; an RNN policy with 1024 parallel environments had mean return 10,070 at the end.
limits: Two value heads did not help when both streams were episodic. Pitfall! still not solved (no positive reward found).
agent_relevance: A knowledge-based bonus that cannot be fooled by noise by construction; the fixed random target fixes the noisy-TV flaw.

source: Savinov et al. (2019) Episodic curiosity through reachability (ECO)
finding: Reward only observations not reachable within k steps from episodic memory. Fixes ICM's tendency to be hooked by controllable randomness.
numbers: DMLab, 20M 4-repeated steps, 30 seeds. Very Sparse: PPO 8.6, PPO+ICM 11.2, PPO+EC 24.7, PPO+ECO 40.5, grid oracle 54.3. Sparse+Doors: 1.5 / 2.7 / 8.5 / 19.8 / 29.4. Dense 1: PPO 22.8, ICM 20.9, ECO 22.9. In VizDoom reaches 100% success at least 2 times faster than ICM.
limits: ICM learned to entertain itself by firing until it ran out of ammunition. Metric on no-reward tasks is coverage, not reward. Authors note a bonus must not hurt dense-reward tasks.
agent_relevance: A memory of what was already seen with a reachability test beats raw prediction error. Maps to a scaffold with a record of visited ideas.

source: Shyam, Jaskowski & Gomez (2019) Model-based active exploration (MAX)
finding: Uses ensemble disagreement and plans for it. Noise shows up as agreement among models, so it is not rewarded; only epistemic uncertainty is.
numbers: Claims at least an order of magnitude better efficiency than strong baselines in semi-random discrete environments needing directed exploration. A stochastic trap state slowed MAX but it still explored the chain.
limits: Evaluated on chains and two MuJoCo tasks with Gaussian N(0,0.02) state noise only.
agent_relevance: Separate I-do-not-know from it-is-random. Our agent can sample several drafts and reward only disagreement that can resolve.

source: Sekar et al. (2020) Plan2Explore
finding: Plans in a learned world model to reach states where an ensemble of latent one-step models disagrees. Explores without reward, then solves downstream tasks zero-shot or few-shot.
numbers: Outperforms prior self-supervised exploration and almost matches an oracle Dreamer with task rewards; beats Dreamer on the hopper hop task. Ensemble of 5 models. Image inputs on DM Control tasks.
limits: Needs a learned world model; results are on simulated control tasks only.
agent_relevance: Planning toward future novelty, not past novelty. Fits a scaffold that predicts which next check will be informative.

source: Colas et al. (2019) CURIOUS: intrinsically motivated modular multi-goal RL
finding: Agent picks which goal module to practise by absolute learning progress, so it spends time on learnable goals and drops solved or impossible ones. Hindsight replay shares data across modules.
numbers: LP of a module is the derivative of competence over a window of self-evaluation rollouts (fraction p_eval=0.1 of episodes). Module sampled with probability proportional to absolute LP. Fetch-arm tasks (Reach, Push, Pick and Place, Stack) with distractors and out-of-reach cubes.
limits: Text notes LP from Bellman errors (Veeriah 2018) did not beat random goal selection. Needs a reliable self-evaluation estimate of competence.
agent_relevance: Absolute LP re-triggers practice when forgetting makes competence fall. A good rule for a reviewing scaffold.

source: Forestier et al. (2022) Intrinsically motivated goal exploration processes with automatic curriculum learning (IMGEP)
finding: IMGEP framework: the learner samples its own goals and picks goal spaces by learning progress. Descendant of Oudeyer's IAC for tool-use and spaces with unlearnable parts.
numbers: JMLR 23 (2022) 1-41; first posted 2017. Specific numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Only the header was checked; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Framework to cite when moving from error-based to goal-based exploration.

source: Pathak et al. (2017) ICM transfer and sanity check
finding: A policy trained by curiosity alone on Mario Level-1 transferred well to Level-3 but not to Level-2 when run as is. Replacing the curiosity net with uniform, Gaussian or Laplacian noise rewards never reached the goal.
numbers: Noise-reward sweep in the sparse VizDoom setup: none of the noise agents reached the goal.
limits: Transfer success tracks visual similarity (Level-3 looks like Level-1; Level-2 does not). Video-based evidence.
agent_relevance: Learned exploration skill transfers only when surface features match; the reward itself is not random-noise driven.

source: Burda et al. (2018) RND episodic vs non-episodic intrinsic return
finding: Treating the intrinsic stream as non-episodic (no reset on death) explored more rooms than episodic in pure-exploration Montezuma runs. A larger intrinsic discount (0.999 vs 0.99) explored more again.
numbers: Non-episodic gamma_I=0.999 explored more rooms than 0.99; one run explored 21 rooms.
limits: Montezuma's Revenge only; a handful of runs per setting.
agent_relevance: Do not let a failed attempt wipe out the credit for novelty already found.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) prediction gain as an approximation of information gain
finding: Information gain is the KL divergence from prior to posterior of a mixture model. Prediction gain (log density after update minus before) approximates it and is a variant of Schmidhuber's compression progress. Pseudo-counts are shown to bound or relate to both.
limits: Theory links hold under density-model assumptions; paper's own tests use Atari frames with a CTS model.
agent_relevance: Learning progress, information gain and counts can be treated as one family, so one cheap proxy may serve all three.
